```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
```

## Problem 1
### Probability that at least two people share a birthday

In this problem, I use simulation to estimate the probability that at least two people share a birthday in a group.

```{r}
birthday_repeated = function(n_people) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_people, replace = TRUE)
  repeated_birthday = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_people
  return(repeated_birthday)
}

birthday_results =
  expand_grid(
    n_people = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(n_people, birthday_repeated)
  )

birthday_summary =
  birthday_results |>
  group_by(n_people) |>
  summarize(
    prob_repeat = mean(repeated)
  )

birthday_repeated(5)
birthday_repeated(23)
birthday_repeated(50)

head(birthday_results, 10)
birthday_summary
```
The simulation results show that the probability of at least two people sharing a birthday increases as the group size increases. For example, the probability is 0.0032 (0.32%) for a group of 2 people, 0.0268 (2.68%) for a group of 5 people, and 0.1168 (11.68%) for a group of 10 people.

```{r}
birthday_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_people, y = prob_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Shared Birthdays",
    x = "Number of People",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  )
```

The plot shows a nonlinear increasing relationship, with the probability reaching approximately 50% at a group size of 23 people and approaching 100% as the group size increases toward 50.

## Problem 2
### A longitudinal study with control and experimental arm

In this problem, I use iteration to import longitudinal data from multiple participants and organize the observations into a tidy dataframe.

```{r}
full_df =
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data/", pattern = "\\.csv$"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    data = map(path, read_csv)
  ) |>
  unnest(data)

tidy_df =
  full_df |>
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, "\\.csv$", ""),
    group = str_sub(files, 1, 3)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(week)
  ) |>
  select(
    group,
    subj = files,
    week,
    outcome
  )

```

```{r}
tidy_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = outcome,
      group = subj,
      color = group
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(
    ~group,
    labeller = as_labeller(
      c(con = "Control", exp = "Experimental")
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Observations by Study Group",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome",
    color = "Study Group"
  )
```

The spaghetti plot shows that the control and experimental groups have different patterns over time. In the control group, outcomes remain relatively stable across the eight weeks, although there are some fluctuations between participants. In the experimental group, outcomes generally increase over time. There are also differences in outcomes among participants within each group. Overall, the experimental group shows a greater increase in outcomes compared to the control group.

## Problem 3
### Simulation to Explore Power in a One-Sample T-Test

In this problem, I use simulation to investigate how the true mean affects statistical power in a one-sample t-test. The sample size is fixed at 30, the standard deviation is fixed at 5, and 5000 datasets are generated for each true mean from 0 to 6.

```{r simulation, cache=TRUE}
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {

  sim_data =
    tibble(
      x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
    )

  test_result =
    t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy()

  return(
    tibble(
      mu_hat = test_result$estimate,
      p_value = test_result$p.value
    )
  )
}

sim_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    estimate_df = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)
  ) |>
  unnest(estimate_df) |>
  mutate(
    reject_null = p_value < 0.05
  )

sim_results_df
```

### Statistical Power

```{r}
power_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject_null)
  )

power_df
```

```{r}
power_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean",
    y = "Proportion of Null Hypotheses Rejected"
  )
```

The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis increases as the true mean moves farther away from zero. When the true mean is zero, approximately 5% of tests are expected to reject the null hypothesis, corresponding to the Type I error rate. As the true mean increases, the effect size becomes larger relative to the fixed standard deviation, resulting in greater statistical power.

### Average Estimated Mean

```{r}
estimate_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_all = mean(mu_hat),
    mean_rejected = mean(mu_hat[reject_null])
  )

estimate_df
```

```{r}
estimate_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    mean_all:mean_rejected,
    names_to = "estimate_type",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = true_mu,
      y = average_estimate,
      color = estimate_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean",
    color = "Estimate Type"
  )
```

The plot shows that the average estimated mean across all samples is very close to the true mean. However, when looking only at samples with significant results, the average estimated mean tends to be higher than the true mean, especially when the true mean is small and positive. As the true mean increases, the difference between the two estimates becomes smaller. This suggests that focusing only on significant results can lead to overestimating the true effect.
